full_text:
Interviewer:	Can you tell me a little bit about what you do?

Subject:	Yes basically I work in an office product delivery unit and our area is very much a development area for upcoming projects, and we launch products, design work, testing, improvements, basically all of that, that I've worked has revolved around photocopiers.

Interviewer:	The questions that I've got are mainly about how your placement relates to your course and how you're getting on with your placement and stuff. So how useful do you think that your course has been to the work that you’re doing?

Subject:	I guess whilst I haven’t really used much of my course the things I have used have obviously been very beneficial, and I’ve used in quite a lot of depth. I think the main difference is the course is very … you're just taught it, whereas once you're at work you obviously get to implement it and then you get real life situations where things don't always go according to plan and then you need to adjust and look broader than just the things that you’re taught.

Interviewer:	Are there any particular skills that you think have been useful?

Subject:	The stuff that I've done has been mainly design work and I know that some of the things I've been taught at uni have been useful in that and applying that. Erm, mechanics particularly and (inaudible) diagrams.

Interviewer:	What about communication skills and more generic stuff – has that been useful?

Subject:	No, to be honest I don't really think that there's been anything from that side of my course that's really benefited me here, but that may be quite a personal thing. Since I've been at work here I've done presentations and been to meetings and suchlike, which I guess some people having done presentations at uni may benefit from that.

Interviewer:	Is there anything you wish you had learnt before you started the placement?

Subject:	No I don't think so, I think the course uni is quite well balanced in that we do get to do some practical application of what we're learning, all be it in a controlled environment, so you know what the outcomes gonna be before you do it, but no I felt quite happy that I haven't really been out of my depth.

Interviewer:	Were you taught anything about health and safety at uni?

Subject:	At uni - only sort of basic things for when we've used workshops etcetera.

Interviewer:	Have you had to do health and safety stuff while you've been here?

Subject:	Yes. We just had to an introduction programme for all the new starts and that involved a health and safety officer speaking to us, explaining and a first aider also spoke to us and explained where the first aid boxes are and how to contact people etcetera. 

Interviewer:	Does it relate at all to what you've done at uni or do you think that health and safety is quite site specific? 

Subject:	I guess it's reasonably site specific, I mean obviously the general gist of it’s the same, but I mean most of it’s kind of common sense anyway. But yes I think being taught what we have at uni, was beneficial in that, obviously it makes you aware, so that's good.

Interviewer:	Ok do you think that the uni could have done more to prepare you for the placement?

Subject:	Not really, I think they did very well actually, to be honest, I found that they were helpful with CV's etcetera, they went through interview technique, and also …

Interviewer:	Do they do that in the department or through the careers service?

Subject:	I actually did it in the department, but I did have my CV checked out of the department.

Interviewer:	How did you find the transition from education to work?

Subject:	It's alright actually, I mean I've obviously worked part-time before, normally holidays, and I would basically work full-time, so it's not been that difficult. I think it's taught me more self-discipline in time management and obviously you can't just kind of fiddle all through the day and do something in the evening, you actually need to be working from when you’re here to when you finish.

Interviewer:	Do you think that will help you when you go back to uni?

Subject:	Definitely, I think it'll give me a lot more structure, yes.

Interviewer:	Have you moved to the area or were you from [name of place]?

Subject:	I've moved to the area here, yes.

Interviewer:	How was that?

Subject:	Yes - it was fine - yeah it was ok. I've lived with a couple of the other girls here that work here, but I hadn’t met them before I moved, [company] helps with that in that they gave us names and addresses of people that were looking for accommodation, so that was beneficial.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you feel like you’ve had to face any new issues since starting? Like office politics or dealing with different types of people?

Subject:	It's obviously been, yeah I mean I obviously there’s been loads of issues in that I’ve dealt with loads of different people, you know concepts, different ideas of how to go about things but nothing that's been too difficult to deal with, it’s been good.

Interviewer:	Now that you’ve spent some time in the work place, how do you think work and university differ?

Subject:	I'd say the work is generally more structured, in that there’s longer term projects, or certainly that's what I've found being here, so it's not just a semester of courses and then you're gonna go and do something totally different. Work is obviously structured in terms of your daily routine, in that when you leave work it's finished, the weekend's yours etcetera.

Interviewer:	Has that made a nice change?

Subject:	Yes, I think I prefer it to be honest. I'd say that - Yeah. What else is different?

Interviewer:	Do you think that work and university have different goals and priorities?

Subject:	Yeah, I guess so, yeah in a way university's kind of training you up for when you take that job, and when you go into that, and work's kind of different in that respect, but then I'm quite lucky in placements, because I've been treated as though I’m just one of the team, so I’m not being differentiated as a student, so that’s good.

Interviewer:	Ok. What sort of proportion of women do they employ here?

Subject:	I don't know obviously actual statistics, but I know that certainly in my department, there's very few women. The financial department and that sort of thing, which have more women go into it. Certainly the engineering side women are a minority.

Interviewer:	Does [company] have a structured programme here for placement students to follow?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	What does that involve?

Subject:	Ok. Basically we have our induction, which includes things like health and safety protection. I think they actually put all the starters through the general programme and then do additional things for industrial placement students. We did a communications workshop, an introduction to basic xerography so that we understand like the structure of the company and where we fit in. They’re very much into meeting your managers to explain where your role is and where you go into the company. And then we have a work (band?) where I've been assigned a tutor from here you does my quarterly reports for IMechE, you have regular appraisals with your manager. Fairly recently I've actually just moved job role which was so that half way through you get to see different business units, so that's all very structured and all of that was outlined at the beginning, you know this is what you’ll be doing, where you'll be going, and these are the targets you’ll be working towards.

Interviewer:	Are you pleased that you have that structure?

Subject:	Yes, yes I think it's be very important, I know they’re do a similar thing for graduates as well, and I think it works very well.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it could be improved in any way?

Subject:	I'm sure it could, I can't actually think of any major improvement that it needs. I mean I've obviously had questions as I’ve gone through but I've always found my manager really approachable and been able to have those answered.

Interviewer:	Is the job that you're doing now, what you expected you would be doing?

Subject:	Yes, I guess on a level it is, I didn't know fully what to expect, but it’s pretty much as I envisioned it. And I got some input into what I would be doing here as well, in that obviously there’s different opportunities and what I focus on, I have a kind of choice.

Interviewer:	Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility?

Subject:	Yes, definitely, they've been very good with giving me responsibility particularly if you can prove that you can cope with it. I get to do presentations for management, to represent my sub-section at daily meetings, to basically be allowed to make decisions and things that I’m capable of doing.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the company have been supportive of you as a placement student?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	How would you summarise your placement experience so far then?

Subject:	I'd say it's been a suitable balance of challenges and the work I've done has been interesting, so that’s good, I'd say mostly generally yeah really happy with my development since I’ve started and the opportunities I’ve been given.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you have changed personally as a result of the placement?

Subject:	I'd say that my goals are still the same, it's just perhaps they are a bit closer. I guess I have changed to some extent, perhaps my confidence, inter-personal skills, having to work round problems, yeah things such as time management, who to go to for certain areas, obviously I’ve found all of that out, and had to sort of push myself to do these things. So, yeah, I guess I probably have changed.

Interviewer:	What would you say have been the best and the worst things about the placement?

Subject:	The worst is you kind of come into it blind and there's so much to learn and there's so much to take in and I'm still learning now and also another kind of negative point I suppose is that everything is very specific to the job that you do this year and if you don't work for the same company then there will be a whole new learning thing to do again after you graduate. The best thing has certainly been the support and the open structure of being able to always speak to your manager or to go higher and have everything answered basically, so that's been a really good structure.

Interviewer:	What would you say are the main benefits of doing the placement? Or do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement?

Subject:	I wouldn't say there's any drawbacks, initially when I thought about getting a placement obviously I realised it would make my degree longer and that was kind of a negative point, but certainly having been here, I think the benefits far outweigh that, because you have a year’s experience. You’ll go back to university more focused because I know really what I want now. And also going back to university with the experience of having worked and dealt with problems is going to make any final year projects or any setbacks and group work far more easy to deal with.

Interviewer:	Are there any other students on placement here? 

Subject:	Yes. They take approximately thirty IPs a year and some of those are in [name]which is a separate business unit. But I’d say probably about 15-20 are taken in (inaudible).

Interviewer:	Did you know any of those students before the start of the placement?

Subject:	There's different areas that they're taken into whether it be finance, software or engineering, integration systems. I had met up with a couple of guys from [university] who are on different courses who have been offered placements, other than that though I didn't know anyone.

Interviewer:	Are the people that you've met male or female?

Subject:	The two people who I met from [university] are both male, they are working on the engineering side, although out of the placement students this year there's about six or seven girls.

Interviewer:	Have you found it beneficial having other students on placement with you?

Subject:	Yeah, I guess because we all did our initial training together. We were split into groups to do like the communication workshop and that sort of thing, which is good.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you feel like you’re treated equally to the other students?

Subject:	Yeah, they're in different teams so it's not really comparable. There are two other mechanical engineers that are basically on a level to me. I mean they do different jobs and their in different teams, but one of them I actually swapped roles with. And I’d say yeah, I think we're treated very much equally.

Interviewer:	Has your work involve a lot of teamwork?

Subject:	Yes, definitely.

Interviewer:	How have you found that?

Subject:	It's obviously got it’s challenges, because as I said earlier people have different ways of approaching things. Meetings can be quite time consuming before decisions are actually made, you might feel like everything's been discussed with no real outcome, which can be a bit frustrating. But certainly working with people in teams, obviously working with permanent employees, has been a really good experience

Interviewer:	How do you think doing team work here compares to doing team work at uni?

Subject:	I guess the biggest thing that I've noticed and that is that everybody here has got the same goal and the same outlook in that they've want to achieve the answer, you know, they're all motivated the same way, whereas at uni when you get in teams there’s normally people who don't wish to pull their weight, which can make it quite difficult, and I'd say it's just got a more mature approach here than in groups at uni.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the group work you do at uni is worthwhile then?

Subject:	Yeah, you certainly learn a lot from group work at uni but on the unfairness side you don't always get recognition that perhaps you deserve or, you know, you’re all marked on a level as a team whereas I'd say in real life, and certainly from my experiences here, when you're working in a team it's obvious who's doing what because you have your own role outlined from the beginning of what you're in charge of and if you don't do that then, then obviously that's noticed when it's reviewed, whereas if you've done the work, then you'll get the recognition for it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that group work at uni could be organised to reflect how it is at work?

Subject:	I think - yeah, there is scope to do that. It's quite a difficult thing to organise because basically it needs overseeing regularly by whoever's gonna mark your group work, I guess, which is quite a time consuming difficult thing to do.

Interviewer:	Have there been any particular people that you’ve liked or disliked working with here?

Subject:	There's obviously been people that I've liked working with and I’d say generally it’s quite a fun environment to work in, there have been not people as such that I’ve disliked working with, but people who have different opinions I guess which has made working with them sometimes a bit awkward, but nothing that's not been overcome.

Interviewer:	Have you been given a mentor?

Subject:	I've got a mentor who he does my quarterly reports for IMechE as I said, who basically kind of oversees that I’m achieving what I need and the goals in terms for that.

Interviewer:	Is that someone outside of your team?

Subject:	He is actually now manager of my team but wasn’t manager of my previous team and I don't work closely with him, although obviously he gets feedback from the people who work under him. But other than that basically I guess our mentor is our manager, that’s who does our regular appraisals and makes sure we’re reaching our goals.

Interviewer:	Do you think it’s a good idea having a more official mentor?

Subject:	I think for me this year it's worked fine, I haven’t needed somebody to actually mentor me as such because I've been able to find people when I need them.

Interviewer:	Ok. Is there anyone else that you go to for advice?

Subject:	In what context?

Interviewer:	Well anything work related, but not necessarily technical stuff …

Subject:	No, not really. There's a learning centre for, you know, if there’s a particular work related thing or if you perhaps want to find out who I would go to rather than through a manager. But no there’s not anybody else.

Interviewer:	Is there anyone that you would say has been like a role model?

Subject:	I think I guess it really is a combination of people that have different characteristics and I'd like to achieve that, I'd like to be there.

Interviewer:	Have you had anyone from uni come to visit you?

Subject:	Yes. I had a lecturer visit once

Interviewer:	Was it a lecturer that you knew?

Subject:	Yes it was, a tutor from uni.

Interviewer:	Did they explain the purpose of the visit?

Subject:	Yes I guess it had been explained to us prior to coming on placement, although I have to say I don't think it has a huge benefit, because they don’t understand what you’re doing in this year and it’s kind of better to have someone closer in the company.

Interviewer:	Did they speak to your manager?

Subject:	Yes, they did yes.

Interviewer:	Would you be happy to go to them if you had any problems? Or would you try and sort it out yourself?

Subject:	To be honest I'd probably sort them out here, because although yeah ok, I've got a mentor at uni, I don't really feel like I'm linked to the university this year, my placement is a work experience and so I kind of feel that if things need sorting, I would do it myself.

Interviewer:	Ok. Are there appropriate facilities here for women?

Subject:	Yep.

Interviewer:	Can you think of any occasions when you think that your gender has determined the reactions you’ve got from people?

Subject:	To be honest, I'd say yes, in that people are obviously aware that you're female. I've never had a negative reaction which has been really good and they certainly don't discriminate in any way. If anything I can perhaps sort of get the appropriate action done sooner. It does work to your advantage.

Interviewer:	So you think it’s been more of an advantage than a disadvantage?

Subject:	Yes, not at any high levels at all, but certainly sort of within the team I guess just general banter, a laugh and a joke. But I know that if I turn up to a team of men to ask for help then I would get it, perhaps as soon if not sooner than a male colleague.

Interviewer:	Ok. So do you think that you want a career in engineering?

Subject:	Yes definitely.

Interviewer:	Has the placement helped make your mind up about what area you'd like to go in or do you think that your career ambitions have changed at all?

Subject:	No I wouldn't say they had changed in terms of what I actually want, I guess a bit more narrowed down to specifics, or I'd be happy to do what I'm doing this year as career.

Interviewer:	Yes. If there was an opportunity to work here, would you?

Subject:	Possibly that’s kind of decided a couple of months before you finish your placement, but depending on obviously how you perform, then that's a possibility.

Interviewer:	If they offered you anything would you accept?

Subject:	I'd certainly consider it yeah.

Interviewer:	So what sort of an area do you think you do want to go into?

Subject:	It’s difficult. erm. I'm currently doing design work which I'm enjoying but that's kind of more for the experience, I quite enjoy the testing side of it but I think to be honest there's still so much that I haven't seen, but I know if I was on a graduate scheme you kind of get to move round and see different areas which would then perhaps help me decide a bit more.

Interviewer:	When you’re looking for a job when you graduate is that the kind of thing you’ll be looking for? A chance to move round?

Subject:	Yes, I think it’d be nice to go onto a programme where you see different areas, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that your placement experience will help you when you start work even if you go into a different area?

Subject:	Yes, yes I think so. I think just in a way that it makes you more aware of how work is sort of expected, just the general structure, maturity I guess.

Interviewer:	Do you think the experience will help you get a job, but also cope in a new work environment?

Subject:	Yes, yes. I think it will. It'll certainly help me get a job even elsewhere because you do have one year’s experience and that’s obviously on your CV and that’s quite a sought after thing in that you’ve got some sort of idea of engineering skills in real like.

Interviewer:	The last questions that I've got to ask you are questions that I asked you last time, just to see if you’re opinion has changed while you’ve been in the industry. So the first one is: Can you think of five words that you would you use to describe the engineering industry or your experience of it?

Subject:	Ok, it's challenging, motivating. It can be, I guess, quite diverse, I've certainly found it very friendly and rewarding.

Interviewer:	Ok. Would you now say that there are any advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in engineering?

Subject:	I don't feel there's been any disadvantages, there's been small advantages in a friendly way, such as like you'll take a drawing to a model shop, and say, you know, can I just drill this, and they’ll sort of offer to do it for you but then I don't see that as a disadvantage because if I wanted to do it I could easily say.

Interviewer:	Do you think it matters that there aren’t more women in engineering?

Subject:	No, I guess I’ve always known when I chose an engineering career that that's how it would be probably for most of my career and that's not really an issue.

Interviewer:	Do you think that it will stay like that?

Subject:	Yes I do. I just - I don't think that's necessarily a bad thing, I just guess it doesn’t really appeal to women.

Interviewer:	In that case do you think that women should be encouraged or enabled to go into engineering?

Subject:	I guess the thing is. I don't really see it as they should be encouraged as such because the opportunities are there, it's not like the avenues are at all closed, it's just obviously there is a lack of interest. I guess it could be promoted more because it isn't specifically a male career but if women don’t want to make that choice that’s kind of their option.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that women aren't interested then?

Subject:	I guess that engineering's kind of portrayed us in cars and engines and motors. If you ask most women they’ll see it as that and I guess that what goes alongside that is the A level choices you make are again very male dominated. You need your maths and physics and they just generally don't appeal, in the same way that less men do English as a degree. I think that that will probably always be there, but women that have probably chosen more scientific based A levels will be aware that engineering isn't all about motors and cars and stuff and that, you know, its much more broader than that and that would be the best thing to promote that it is actually broader than that, that there's more available than what people initially think I guess.

Interviewer:	That’s it thank you.

turns.text: Is the job that you're doing now, what you expected you would be doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I guess on a level it is, I didn't know fully what to expect, but it’s pretty much as I envisioned it. And I got some input into what I would be doing here as well, in that obviously there’s different opportunities and what I focus on, I have a kind of choice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, definitely, they've been very good with giving me responsibility particularly if you can prove that you can cope with it. I get to do presentations for management, to represent my sub-section at daily meetings, to basically be allowed to make decisions and things that I’m capable of doing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the company have been supportive of you as a placement student?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How would you summarise your placement experience so far then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'd say it's been a suitable balance of challenges and the work I've done has been interesting, so that’s good, I'd say mostly generally yeah really happy with my development since I’ve started and the opportunities I’ve been given.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you have changed personally as a result of the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'd say that my goals are still the same, it's just perhaps they are a bit closer. I guess I have changed to some extent, perhaps my confidence, inter-personal skills, having to work round problems, yeah things such as time management, who to go to for certain areas, obviously I’ve found all of that out, and had to sort of push myself to do these things. So, yeah, I guess I probably have changed.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would you say have been the best and the worst things about the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The worst is you kind of come into it blind and there's so much to learn and there's so much to take in and I'm still learning now and also another kind of negative point I suppose is that everything is very specific to the job that you do this year and if you don't work for the same company then there will be a whole new learning thing to do again after you graduate. The best thing has certainly been the support and the open structure of being able to always speak to your manager or to go higher and have everything answered basically, so that's been a really good structure.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would you say are the main benefits of doing the placement? Or do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I wouldn't say there's any drawbacks, initially when I thought about getting a placement obviously I realised it would make my degree longer and that was kind of a negative point, but certainly having been here, I think the benefits far outweigh that, because you have a year’s experience. You’ll go back to university more focused because I know really what I want now. And also going back to university with the experience of having worked and dealt with problems is going to make any final year projects or any setbacks and group work far more easy to deal with.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are there any other students on placement here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. They take approximately thirty IPs a year and some of those are in [name]which is a separate business unit. But I’d say probably about 15-20 are taken in (inaudible).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you know any of those students before the start of the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There's different areas that they're taken into whether it be finance, software or engineering, integration systems. I had met up with a couple of guys from [university] who are on different courses who have been offered placements, other than that though I didn't know anyone.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are the people that you've met male or female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The two people who I met from [university] are both male, they are working on the engineering side, although out of the placement students this year there's about six or seven girls.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you found it beneficial having other students on placement with you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I guess because we all did our initial training together. We were split into groups to do like the communication workshop and that sort of thing, which is good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, do you feel like you’re treated equally to the other students?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, they're in different teams so it's not really comparable. There are two other mechanical engineers that are basically on a level to me. I mean they do different jobs and their in different teams, but one of them I actually swapped roles with. And I’d say yeah, I think we're treated very much equally.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has your work involve a lot of teamwork?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How have you found that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It's obviously got it’s challenges, because as I said earlier people have different ways of approaching things. Meetings can be quite time consuming before decisions are actually made, you might feel like everything's been discussed with no real outcome, which can be a bit frustrating. But certainly working with people in teams, obviously working with permanent employees, has been a really good experience

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you think doing team work here compares to doing team work at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I guess the biggest thing that I've noticed and that is that everybody here has got the same goal and the same outlook in that they've want to achieve the answer, you know, they're all motivated the same way, whereas at uni when you get in teams there’s normally people who don't wish to pull their weight, which can make it quite difficult, and I'd say it's just got a more mature approach here than in groups at uni.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the group work you do at uni is worthwhile then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, you certainly learn a lot from group work at uni but on the unfairness side you don't always get recognition that perhaps you deserve or, you know, you’re all marked on a level as a team whereas I'd say in real life, and certainly from my experiences here, when you're working in a team it's obvious who's doing what because you have your own role outlined from the beginning of what you're in charge of and if you don't do that then, then obviously that's noticed when it's reviewed, whereas if you've done the work, then you'll get the recognition for it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that group work at uni could be organised to reflect how it is at work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think - yeah, there is scope to do that. It's quite a difficult thing to organise because basically it needs overseeing regularly by whoever's gonna mark your group work, I guess, which is quite a time consuming difficult thing to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have there been any particular people that you’ve liked or disliked working with here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There's obviously been people that I've liked working with and I’d say generally it’s quite a fun environment to work in, there have been not people as such that I’ve disliked working with, but people who have different opinions I guess which has made working with them sometimes a bit awkward, but nothing that's not been overcome.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you been given a mentor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I've got a mentor who he does my quarterly reports for IMechE as I said, who basically kind of oversees that I’m achieving what I need and the goals in terms for that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that someone outside of your team?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: He is actually now manager of my team but wasn’t manager of my previous team and I don't work closely with him, although obviously he gets feedback from the people who work under him. But other than that basically I guess our mentor is our manager, that’s who does our regular appraisals and makes sure we’re reaching our goals.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’s a good idea having a more official mentor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think for me this year it's worked fine, I haven’t needed somebody to actually mentor me as such because I've been able to find people when I need them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Is there anyone else that you go to for advice?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In what context?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well anything work related, but not necessarily technical stuff …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, not really. There's a learning centre for, you know, if there’s a particular work related thing or if you perhaps want to find out who I would go to rather than through a manager. But no there’s not anybody else.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anyone that you would say has been like a role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think I guess it really is a combination of people that have different characteristics and I'd like to achieve that, I'd like to be there.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had anyone from uni come to visit you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. I had a lecturer visit once

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was it a lecturer that you knew?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes it was, a tutor from uni.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did they explain the purpose of the visit?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes I guess it had been explained to us prior to coming on placement, although I have to say I don't think it has a huge benefit, because they don’t understand what you’re doing in this year and it’s kind of better to have someone closer in the company.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did they speak to your manager?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, they did yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you be happy to go to them if you had any problems? Or would you try and sort it out yourself?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: To be honest I'd probably sort them out here, because although yeah ok, I've got a mentor at uni, I don't really feel like I'm linked to the university this year, my placement is a work experience and so I kind of feel that if things need sorting, I would do it myself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Are there appropriate facilities here for women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yep.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Can you think of any occasions when you think that your gender has determined the reactions you’ve got from people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: To be honest, I'd say yes, in that people are obviously aware that you're female. I've never had a negative reaction which has been really good and they certainly don't discriminate in any way. If anything I can perhaps sort of get the appropriate action done sooner. It does work to your advantage.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you think it’s been more of an advantage than a disadvantage?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, not at any high levels at all, but certainly sort of within the team I guess just general banter, a laugh and a joke. But I know that if I turn up to a team of men to ask for help then I would get it, perhaps as soon if not sooner than a male colleague.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. So do you think that you want a career in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has the placement helped make your mind up about what area you'd like to go in or do you think that your career ambitions have changed at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No I wouldn't say they had changed in terms of what I actually want, I guess a bit more narrowed down to specifics, or I'd be happy to do what I'm doing this year as career.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes. If there was an opportunity to work here, would you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Possibly that’s kind of decided a couple of months before you finish your placement, but depending on obviously how you perform, then that's a possibility.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If they offered you anything would you accept?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'd certainly consider it yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So what sort of an area do you think you do want to go into?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s difficult. erm. I'm currently doing design work which I'm enjoying but that's kind of more for the experience, I quite enjoy the testing side of it but I think to be honest there's still so much that I haven't seen, but I know if I was on a graduate scheme you kind of get to move round and see different areas which would then perhaps help me decide a bit more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: When you’re looking for a job when you graduate is that the kind of thing you’ll be looking for? A chance to move round?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think it’d be nice to go onto a programme where you see different areas, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that your placement experience will help you when you start work even if you go into a different area?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, yes I think so. I think just in a way that it makes you more aware of how work is sort of expected, just the general structure, maturity I guess.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think the experience will help you get a job, but also cope in a new work environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, yes. I think it will. It'll certainly help me get a job even elsewhere because you do have one year’s experience and that’s obviously on your CV and that’s quite a sought after thing in that you’ve got some sort of idea of engineering skills in real like.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: The last questions that I've got to ask you are questions that I asked you last time, just to see if you’re opinion has changed while you’ve been in the industry. So the first one is: Can you think of five words that you would you use to describe the engineering industry or your experience of it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ok, it's challenging, motivating. It can be, I guess, quite diverse, I've certainly found it very friendly and rewarding.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Would you now say that there are any advantages or disadvantages to being a woman in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't feel there's been any disadvantages, there's been small advantages in a friendly way, such as like you'll take a drawing to a model shop, and say, you know, can I just drill this, and they’ll sort of offer to do it for you but then I don't see that as a disadvantage because if I wanted to do it I could easily say.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it matters that there aren’t more women in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I guess I’ve always known when I chose an engineering career that that's how it would be probably for most of my career and that's not really an issue.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that it will stay like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes I do. I just - I don't think that's necessarily a bad thing, I just guess it doesn’t really appeal to women.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: In that case do you think that women should be encouraged or enabled to go into engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I guess the thing is. I don't really see it as they should be encouraged as such because the opportunities are there, it's not like the avenues are at all closed, it's just obviously there is a lack of interest. I guess it could be promoted more because it isn't specifically a male career but if women don’t want to make that choice that’s kind of their option.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that women aren't interested then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I guess that engineering's kind of portrayed us in cars and engines and motors. If you ask most women they’ll see it as that and I guess that what goes alongside that is the A level choices you make are again very male dominated. You need your maths and physics and they just generally don't appeal, in the same way that less men do English as a degree. I think that that will probably always be there, but women that have probably chosen more scientific based A levels will be aware that engineering isn't all about motors and cars and stuff and that, you know, its much more broader than that and that would be the best thing to promote that it is actually broader than that, that there's more available than what people initially think I guess.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s it thank you.
